adults.title: Worth the Voyage
adults.big_idea: Living apostles and prophets are a gift from the Savior that was missing from the earth for centuries, and we honor that gift by refusing to treat their words as a light thing.
adults.objective: Learners will feel fresh gratitude for living prophets, seers, and revelators and will choose one specific way to give their words more weight this week.
prepare: Read Elder Sikahema’s talk, especially the story of his grandparents’ voyage (the first eleven paragraphs).
Mark Amos 8:11–12, Amos 3:7, Doctrine and Covenants 90:5 and Doctrine and Covenants 1:38.
Bring paper and pens for silent writing.
Write on the board: 16 hours. Two and a half days. One tap.
Be aware that the story includes the death of a baby. Someone in the room may carry a similar loss; tell it simply and reverently.

segments.name: What would you cross an ocean for?
steps: Begin with prayer. If you wish, sing the hymn listed under music.
Ask the first question below and let learners answer in pairs for one minute. Take two or three answers aloud.
Point to the board. Explain that today’s talk tells of a family for whom hearing an Apostle cost two and a half days at sea and far more, while for us it usually costs one tap on a phone.
Say that Elder Sikahema of the Seventy told this story about his own grandparents.
questions: What is the greatest effort you have ever made to be in the room with someone or to hear something in person? Why was it worth it to you?

segments.name: The Wolfgramms’ voyage
steps: Retell the story in your own words, or have three readers share the paragraphs that tell it. Keep to the details: in 1947 Sione and Salote Wolfgramm, poor farmers serving a mission on the isolated island of Niuatoputapu in Tonga, set out with their three small children to reach Elder Matthew Cowley, an Apostle. Only two Apostles had ever visited Tonga before.

Continue: a voyage of 16 hours to their home island of Vava‘u became two and a half days in a storm. Their nine-month-old son, Vilimanulea, died of exposure. Within two days they buried him and continued their voyage.
Read the first two key quotes aloud, slowly. Allow a moment of quiet.
Ask the questions below. Do not hurry the silence after the first one.
questions: What do you feel as you picture them getting back on the boat?
According to Elder Sikahema, what did his grandparents understand about an Apostle that made them keep sailing?

segments.name: Famine and feast
steps: Divide into small groups. Give half the groups Amos 8:11–12 and the other half Amos 3:7. Ask each group to read its passage and agree on one sentence: what does this teach about why prophets matter?
Have a spokesperson from each side report. Write the two sentences side by side on the board under the words Famine and Feast.

Explain what Elder Sikahema taught: for centuries after the ancient apostles died there was no revelation to prophets, and reformers yearned for prophetic voices but could not find them, until the Father and the Son appeared to Joseph Smith.
Read President Holland’s question and answer, which Elder Sikahema quoted (see aligned quotes). Ask the question below.
questions: When has the word of the Lord through a living prophet or apostle reached you at a time you were hungry for it?

segments.name: A light thing, or a weighty one
steps: Read Doctrine and Covenants 90:5 together. Then read the key quote about cell phones.
Give each person paper. Invite three minutes of silent writing on the two prompts below. Tell them no one will collect it.
Invite a few who are willing to share one thing they wrote for the second prompt. List their ideas on the board.
Read the speaker’s invitation word for word (see invitations). Then read President Oaks’s invitation from the close of this conference (see aligned quotes) and note how the two fit together.
questions: Where has the ease of hearing prophets made me casual about what they say?
What would it look like, in my real week, to hold their words as a weighty thing?

segments.name: Choose, and trust His word
steps: Read Doctrine and Covenants 1:38. Point out the promise in it that the speaker quoted: the Lord’s word will all be fulfilled, whether it comes by His own voice or by the voice of His servants.
As a check for understanding, ask each person to finish this sentence on their paper: Holding the words of prophets as a weighty thing means that this week I will…
Invite them to turn to a neighbor and say their sentence aloud.
Bear your testimony of the Savior and of His living prophets, seers, and revelators, as Elder Sikahema did.
Tell the class that next week you will begin by asking two or three people what they did and what they noticed. Write yourself a reminder so that you do.

key_quotes.text: Grieving with empty arms, my grandparents got back on the boat, their mission not yet complete.
They sailed to sit at the feet of an Apostle, who would teach them their duty so they could bless others on their island with the message of the restored gospel of Jesus Christ.
I suspect the Lord knew that even when we would have these devices (cell phones) to easily see and hear His anointed servants, many of us would still take them for granted.
What a blessing it is to live in a time when apostles and prophets are on the earth.

scriptures.use: Half the small groups read it and write one sentence on what a world without prophetic revelation is like.
The other groups read it and write one sentence on how the Lord chooses to work; compare the two sentences on the board.
Read together before the silent writing; ask what makes a sacred thing become a light thing to us.
Read at the close as the Lord’s assurance that the words of His servants will be fulfilled.

aligned_quotes.text: Are the heavens open? Does God reveal His will to prophets and apostles as in days of old? That they are and that He does is the unflinching declaration of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints to all the world.
aligned_quotes.speaker: President Jeffrey R. Holland
President Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: As the talks of this conference are published, we invite all to study and ponder them prayerfully and to act in faith on the principles they explain.

invitations.text: let us not be guilty of holding “the oracles of God … as a light thing”

takeaways: Living apostles and prophets are a gift the world went without for centuries.
What costs us one tap cost others an ocean; ease must not become indifference.
The Lord’s word through His servants will all be fulfilled, so it deserves real weight in my week.
act: Choose one talk from this conference by a prophet, seer, and revelator and study it this week with a pen in hand, writing down one thing to do.
Set a fixed time and place for that study, with other apps closed, as a way of giving the words weight.
Tell a family member or friend one sentence from a living prophet that has fed you, and why.
In your prayers this week, thank Heavenly Father by name for living prophets and apostles.
music: We Thank Thee, O God, for a Prophet
adapt: At home: tell the story at the table, read Doctrine and Covenants 90:5, and let each person answer the second writing prompt aloud instead of on paper.
Large class: do the Amos readings in pairs with the person beside them rather than moving into groups.
Short on time: keep the voyage, Doctrine and Covenants 90:5 with the silent writing, and the closing choice; drop the Amos group work and simply summarize it.

youth.title: Two and a Half Days, or One Tap
youth.big_idea: Having living prophets and apostles is a rare gift, and the fact that we can hear them so easily is no reason to treat what they say lightly.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to explain why living prophets are a gift worth sacrifice and will plan one specific way to take a prophet’s words seriously this week.
prepare: Read Elder Sikahema’s talk. Practice retelling his grandparents’ voyage in about three minutes.
Ask the youth ahead of time to bring phones or scriptures. Have a timer ready.
Bring paper and markers for three teams.
Write on the board, covered or turned away until needed: 16 hours. Two and a half days.

segments.name: The race
steps: Start right after the prayer. Say: phones or scriptures out. On go, find any talk from this general conference by a member of the First Presidency or the Twelve and hold it up. Go.
Time the first person and the last person. Write both times on the board in seconds.

Uncover the other numbers on the board. Explain that in 1947 a young couple in Tonga expected a 16-hour voyage toward an Apostle and it became two and a half days in a storm. Today’s lesson is about the gap between those numbers and yours.

segments.name: The voyage
steps: Tell the story, keeping to Elder Sikahema’s details: his grandparents, Sione and Salote Wolfgramm, were 28 and 25, poor farmers with no formal education, serving a mission on the isolated island of Niuatoputapu with three children aged 4, 3 and 9 months. Elder Matthew Cowley, an Apostle, was coming to Tonga. Only two Apostles had ever visited before.
Tell the hard part honestly and gently: the storm left their baby son severely dehydrated, there was no medicine, and he died. They buried him within two days and continued their voyage.
Have a youth read the key quote that calls an Apostle’s visit the chance of a lifetime. Then have another read the paragraph of the talk that begins: They were sailing toward an Apostle.
Ask the questions below. Let them answer each other, not just you.
questions: Be honest: what is your first reaction to their choice to keep going?
What did they believe an Apostle had that they could not get anywhere else?

segments.name: Headline challenge
steps: Make three teams. Team 1 reads Amos 8:11–12. Team 2 reads Amos 3:7. Team 3 reads Joseph Smith—History 1:17.
Each team has three minutes to write a headline of eight words or fewer that captures its passage, in big letters on paper.
Teams hold up and explain their headlines in the order 1, 2, 3. The class votes for the best one that is not their own.

Connect the three: a long famine of hearing the Lord’s word; the Lord’s pattern of revealing through prophets; and the day the heavens opened to a teenager. Read the key quote about a then-teenage boy.
Read President Holland’s words quoted in the talk (see aligned quotes).
questions: The Father and the Son began the Restoration through someone about your age. What does that say about how the Lord sees young people?

segments.name: A light thing?
steps: Read Doctrine and Covenants 90:5 aloud. Explain simply that the Lord is warning us not to treat lightly what He reveals through His servants.
Have a youth read the key quote about cell phones. Hold up your own phone as you ask the first question.

Movement: name one wall Agree and the opposite wall Disagree. Read each statement below and have the youth move, then ask one person from each side why. Statements: The easier something is to get, the less I value it. I remember more from a talk when I write something down. It is harder to listen to a prophet when I already think I know what he will say.
Have everyone sit. Read the speaker’s invitation word for word (see invitations).
questions: Why do we take for granted the things that are easiest to reach?
How can a person your age know for themselves that prophets speak for the Lord? What has helped you?

segments.name: Make it weigh something
steps: In pairs, give two minutes to design a one-week plan that would make a prophet’s words heavy instead of light for a teenager. It must be specific and realistic: which talk, when, where, and what you will do with it.
Hear plans quickly. Let the group choose one to do together, or let each youth choose their own.
Have each youth write their plan in their phone notes or on paper and show it to their partner. This is your check that everyone has one.
Read Doctrine and Covenants 1:38 and point out the Lord’s assurance, which the speaker quoted, that His word will all be fulfilled whether by His own voice or the voice of His servants.

segments.name: Witness and follow-up
steps: Read the key quote that begins: What a blessing it is. Bear brief testimony of Jesus Christ and of His living prophets.
Tell the youth you will open next week by asking what they did and what they noticed. During the week, send one short reminder to the class or to their parents.

key_quotes.text: For Saints scattered across the Pacific, having an Apostle of the Lord among them was the chance of a lifetime.
I suspect the Lord knew that even when we would have these devices (cell phones) to easily see and hear His anointed servants, many of us would still take them for granted.

With that clear, simple, and understated introduction, the Father and His Son, Jesus Christ, would begin the work of restoring the Savior’s ancient Church through a then-teenage boy in upstate New York.
What a blessing it is to live in a time when apostles and prophets are on the earth.

scriptures.use: Team 1 reads it and writes a headline of eight words or fewer about a world hungry for the Lord’s word.
Team 2 reads it and writes a headline about how the Lord reveals His will.
Team 3 reads it and writes a headline about the day the heavens opened to a teenager.
Read aloud before the Agree and Disagree activity; ask what treating revelation as a light thing looks like at their age.

aligned_quotes.text: Are the heavens open? Does God reveal His will to prophets and apostles as in days of old? That they are and that He does is the unflinching declaration of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints to all the world.
aligned_quotes.speaker: President Jeffrey R. Holland
Elder Caussé
aligned_quotes.text: Apostles bear a unique, authoritative, divinely empowered witness of the living Christ

invitations.text: let us not be guilty of holding “the oracles of God … as a light thing”

takeaways: For centuries people longed for prophets and could not find them; we have them.
Easy to reach does not mean small.
The Lord began the Restoration through a teenager, and He speaks to me through His prophets today.
act: Pick one talk from this conference by a prophet, seer, and revelator. Listen to it this week with nothing else on your screen, and write down one sentence to act on.
Put that one sentence where you will see it every day, such as your lock screen or mirror, and do what it says.
Tell one friend or family member what you chose and why.
Thank Heavenly Father in prayer for living prophets, and ask Him to help you know their words are true.
music: We Thank Thee, O God, for a Prophet
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: skip the teams; read each of the three passages together and write one headline for each as a family.
Large class: make six teams, two for each passage, and let the pairs of teams compete for the better headline.
Only 15 minutes: do the race, the voyage, Doctrine and Covenants 90:5 with the phone quote, and the one-week plan.

children.title: I Can Listen to the Prophet
children.big_idea: Heavenly Father loves us, so He gives us prophets and apostles who teach us about Jesus Christ, and I can listen to them.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that Heavenly Father speaks to us through prophets and will choose one way to listen to the prophet this week.
prepare: Read Elder Sikahema’s talk. In this lesson, tell only the part about the family sailing through a storm to hear an Apostle; leave out the death of the baby.
Bring a blanket or large towel, a flashlight, paper and crayons.
Bring a picture of the living prophet, or have one ready on a phone.
Clear a space on the floor large enough for all the children to sit on the blanket.

segments.name: Come close to hear
steps: After the prayer, stand far from the children and whisper very softly: Heavenly Father loves you. Ask whether they could hear.
Invite them to tiptoe close and whisper it again. Ask what they did to hear better.
Show the picture of the prophet. Say today’s truth and have the children repeat it with you twice: Heavenly Father speaks to us through prophets.

segments.name: The boat and the storm
steps: Spread the blanket on the floor. This is the boat. Invite everyone aboard.

Tell the story simply: a long time ago, on a small island in Tonga, in the great Pacific Ocean, lived Elder Sikahema’s grandparents. They were missionaries. They heard that an Apostle of Jesus Christ, Elder Matthew Cowley, was coming. An Apostle had come to their islands only two times before. They wanted very much to hear him, so they got on a boat with their little children.

Have the children sway gently as the boat sails. Then tell them a storm came. Sway more, pat knees for rain, hug arms for cold. The trip should have taken 16 hours. It took two and a half days. They were soaked and sick. It was very hard and very sad.
Become still. Say: they did not give up. They kept sailing to hear the Apostle. Ask the questions below.
questions: Why do you think they wanted so much to hear an Apostle?
Who do Apostles and prophets teach us about?

segments.name: The light comes on
steps: Stay on the blanket. Dim the lights if the children are comfortable with that. Explain that for a very long time there were no prophets on the earth, and people who wanted to hear God’s word could not find it.

Tell them a boy named Joseph Smith prayed. Turn on the flashlight and shine it on the ceiling. Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ came to him in bright light. Heavenly Father pointed to Jesus and spoke. Read His words from the key quotes and have the children repeat the last two words: Hear Him.
Turn the lights back on. Say that because of that day we have prophets and apostles again, and today’s prophet helps us hear Jesus.
Repeat together: Heavenly Father speaks to us through prophets.

segments.name: Freeze and listen
steps: Have the children walk quietly around the room. Tell them that when you say something prophets teach, they freeze, cup a hand to an ear, and say it back.
Speak in a normal voice at first, then more softly each time so they must listen harder: Jesus loves you. Pray every day. Be kind. Read the scriptures. Love your family.
Sing “Follow the Prophet” (the chorus is enough) as they walk back to their seats.

segments.name: Draw how I listen
steps: Give each child paper and crayons. Ask them to draw themselves listening to the prophet. Offer ideas: listening at general conference, hearing a story about the prophet, or doing something the prophet teaches, such as praying or being kind.
As they draw, go to each child and ask them to tell you about the picture. This is how you check what each one understood.
Write on each paper, or let children who can write do it: I can listen to the prophet.
Let two or three children show their drawings and say the words on the paper.

segments.name: Choose and close
steps: Remind them that the family in the story sailed for days to hear an Apostle. We can hear the prophet very easily, and that is a blessing. Read the key quote that begins: What a blessing it is.
Ask each child to choose one way to listen this week and say it aloud: I will listen to the prophet by…
Bear a short testimony that Heavenly Father loves them and that Jesus Christ leads His Church through living prophets.
Ask them to take their drawings home and tell someone the story of the boat. Tell them you will ask next week what they did, and begin next week by asking.
Say the truth together one last time and close with prayer.

key_quotes.text: What a blessing it is to live in a time when apostles and prophets are on the earth.
This is My Beloved Son. Hear Him!
having an Apostle of the Lord among them was the chance of a lifetime

scriptures.use: Tell the children in your own words that the Lord tells His prophets what He wants us to know; an older child may read the verse aloud.
Use during the flashlight activity; read the Father’s words from the key quotes and have the children repeat the last two.
For older children: read it aloud and ask whose voice we hear when the Lord’s servants speak His word.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Caussé
aligned_quotes.text: Apostles bear a unique, authoritative, divinely empowered witness of the living Christ

takeaways: Heavenly Father speaks to us through prophets.
Prophets and apostles teach us about Jesus Christ.
I can listen to the prophet.
act: Listen to or read one short part of a general conference talk by the prophet with a grown-up, and say one thing you heard.
Do one thing prophets teach, such as praying each day or being kind to someone.
Show your drawing at home and tell the story of the family who sailed through a storm to hear an Apostle.
music: We Thank Thee, O God, for a Prophet

adapt.younger: For ages 3–7: keep the story to about two minutes and let the swaying, rain and cold actions carry it. Repeat the truth after every activity. Give each child a helper job, such as holding the flashlight, holding the picture of the prophet, or passing out crayons. For the drawing, it is enough to draw a face with big listening ears. If dimming the lights worries anyone, leave them on.
adapt.older: For ages 8–11: invite one child to read Amos 3:7 and another Joseph Smith—History 1:17 aloud. Let an older child lead the freeze and listen game. Ask a harder question: hearing the prophet is easy for us, so how do we keep from forgetting how special it is? Share Elder Caussé’s words about the witness of Apostles (see aligned quotes) and ask what an Apostle is a witness of.
